q: The AI Act is a regulation, yet its enforcement stalled in several Member States during 2025-26. The reason was that:
a: national parliaments still had to transpose the Regulation into domestic law before it could bind providers
b: Member States must designate and resource notifying and market surveillance authorities, and many did so late
c: the Court of Justice suspended the Regulation's application pending a challenge to its chosen legal basis
d: the Regulation's prohibitions were held in abeyance until harmonised standards were cited in the Official Journal
explain: A regulation applies directly, but Chapter VII still requires each Member State to designate and equip notifying and market surveillance authorities; by 2026 only a minority had both in place. Transposition is not the issue — a regulation needs none, unlike NIS2.

sources.quote: Each Member State shall establish or designate as national competent authorities at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation.

the delayed availability of standards, common specifications, and alternative guidance and the delayed establishment of national competent authorities lead to challenges that jeopardise the effective entry into application of those obligations

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026. Its central effect on the AI Act was to:
a: repeal the high-risk chapter and put a voluntary conformity scheme in its place for Annex III systems
b: transfer enforcement of the general-purpose AI chapter from the Commission to national market surveillance authorities
c: defer application of the high-risk obligations while leaving the prohibitions and the general-purpose AI chapter in place
d: bring the transparency obligations for synthetic content forward so that they applied from the date of entry into force
explain: The Omnibus pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028, while Article 5 and Chapter V continued to apply. Deferral is not repeal: conformity assessment remains mandatory once the new dates arrive.

sources.quote: Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I;
This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

q: Besides Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 itself, the Digital Omnibus on AI amended:
a: the Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 and the NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555
b: the EASA Basic Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 and the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230
c: the Digital Services Act (EU) 2022/2065 and the Digital Markets Act (EU) 2022/1925
d: the Data Governance Act (EU) 2022/868 and the Data Act (EU) 2023/2854
explain: Articles 2 and 3 of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amend the EASA Basic Regulation, so that acts on AI safety components take the AI Act's high-risk requirements into account, and the Machinery Regulation, which moves to Section B of AI Act Annex I and must absorb AI health-and-safety requirements through delegated acts applying by 2 August 2028. The data and platform acquis was not touched by this instrument.

sources.quote: amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
it is appropriate to move to a sectoral approach by moving Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 from Section A to Section B of Annex I to Regulation (EU) 2024/1689

q: The 'small mid-cap' category now referred to in the AI Act:
a: was defined in Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 and applied to the AI Act by the Digital Omnibus
b: was created by the AI Act itself and covers any provider employing fewer than 250 persons in the Union
c: was introduced by the Data Act and determines which providers get priority access to regulatory sandboxes
d: applies only to providers of general-purpose AI models that stay below the systemic-risk compute threshold
explain: The category comes from the Commission's 2025 simplification agenda — an enterprise that is not an SME, employs fewer than 750 people and stays under €150 million turnover or €129 million balance sheet — and reached the AI Act only through Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Fewer than 250 employees is the SME ceiling, not the small mid-cap one.

sources.quote: “small mid-cap enterprise” or “SMC” means a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (2) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099;

it is necessary to introduce definitions for SMEs and SMCs, which should correspond to the definition set out in the Annex to Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC (6) and Annex to Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 (7), respectively.

q: A manufacturer wants to use sensor data from machines it has sold to train a predictive-maintenance model. The instrument that most directly governs whether the machines' users can obtain that same data is:
a: the Data Governance Act, which sets the conditions for re-use of protected public sector data holdings
b: the AI Act, which requires providers of high-risk systems to use relevant and representative training data
c: the Data Act, which gives users of connected products access to the data they generate and rights to share it
d: the GDPR, which lets data subjects obtain personal data concerning them in a structured machine-readable format
explain: The Data Act's core right, applicable since 12 September 2025, is user access to connected-product data and onward sharing with third parties of the user's choice. Portability under the GDPR is the closest alternative but covers only personal data of the data subject, whereas machine telemetry is largely non-personal industrial data.

sources.quote: Where data cannot be directly accessed by the user from the connected product or related service, data holders shall make readily available data, as well as the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data, accessible to the user without undue delay

Upon request by a user, or by a party acting on behalf of a user, the data holder shall make available readily available data, as well as the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data, to a third party without undue delay

q: The Data Act's chapter on data-processing services obliges providers to:
a: keep all data belonging to customers established in the Union stored and processed on Union territory
b: obtain authorisation from the national market surveillance authority before offering services in a Member State
c: notify the Commission of every processing operation carried out on behalf of a public sector customer
d: remove contractual, commercial and technical obstacles to switching, and phase out switching charges
explain: Switching and interoperability are the Data Act's answer to cloud lock-in, with switching charges withdrawn after a transition period. Data localisation was deliberately not adopted — the Act addresses portability, and separately restricts unlawful third-country access to non-personal data held in the Union.

sources.quote: In particular, providers of data processing services shall not impose and shall remove pre-commercial, commercial, technical, contractual and organisational obstacles, which inhibit customers from:
From 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services shall not impose any switching charges on the customer for the switching process.

q: The Data Governance Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/868) established:
a: a notification regime for data intermediation services and a voluntary register of recognised data altruism organisations
b: a right for users to access the data generated by the connected products they own, rent or lease
c: a single European register of all personal data processing carried out by public sector bodies
d: mandatory open licensing of every category of public sector information held by national administrations
explain: The DGA is the trust framework: neutral intermediaries, altruistic data donation, and conditions for re-using protected public sector data. Connected-product access rights belong to the Data Act, adopted a year later, which is the usual confusion.

sources.quote: a notification and supervisory framework for the provision of data intermediation services; (c) a framework for voluntary registration of entities which collect and process data made available for altruistic purposes
Each competent authority for the registration of data altruism organisations shall keep and regularly update a public national register of recognised data altruism organisations.

q: Common European data spaces are best described as:
a: certified cloud regions in which service providers must host all data originating within the Union
b: national data registers that Member States are required to notify to the Commission under the Data Act
c: sector-specific federated ecosystems in which participants share data under common governance and interoperability rules
d: centralised Union repositories into which sectoral data is pooled and which the Commission operates under a single access regime
explain: Data spaces are federated by design: data stays with its holders and is shared under agreed rules, with the European Health Data Space the first one put into legislation. There is no central Commission-run pool — that model was rejected as unworkable for sensitive sectoral data.

sources.quote: common European data spaces, namely purpose- or sector-specific or cross-sectoral interoperable frameworks of common standards and practices to share or jointly process data
the Commission proposed establishing domain-specific common European data spaces for data sharing and data pooling

q: For a research team seeking EU-wide health data to train a clinical model, the European Health Data Space matters mainly because it:
a: obliges hospitals to publish anonymised patient records in an openly accessible repository from 2027
b: removes the need for a lawful basis under data-protection law where the purpose of processing is research
c: makes approval by a research ethics committee sufficient for cross-border transfers of clinical records
d: creates a permit-based secondary-use regime run by health data access bodies, phased in from around 2029
explain: The EHDS builds a governed route to secondary use: applicants ask a health data access body for a data permit, with the main secondary-use provisions applying from around 2029. It does not displace data-protection law, which continues to apply alongside it.

sources.quote: health data holders should make the data they hold available on the basis of a data permit or a health data request. For the purpose of processing electronic health data for secondary use, one of the legal bases referred to in Article 6(1), points (a), (c), (e) or (f), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 in conjunction with Article 9(2) thereof is required.
Chapter IV shall apply from 26 March 2029. However, Article 55(6), Article 70, Article 73(5), Article 75(1) and (12), Article 77(4) and Article 78(6) shall apply from 26 March 2027

q: A very large platform runs a recommender system driven by a large model. The division of labour between the DSA and the AI Act is that:
a: both apply, but the DSA prevails as lex specialis for any service designated as very large
b: the DSA governs the platform's systemic risks and recommender transparency, while the AI Act governs the AI system as a product
c: the AI Act applies to the model and displaces the DSA obligations in respect of that part of the service, which is treated as a product
d: the DSA reaches only content moderation decisions, leaving recommender systems entirely to the AI Act
explain: The two act cumulatively on different objects: service-level duties under the DSA, product-level duties under the AI Act. Neither displaces the other, so one recommender can be a DSA systemic-risk factor and an AI system within the AI Act's scope at the same time.

sources.quote: thereby complementing obligations for providers of intermediary services that embed such systems or models into their services regulated by Regulation (EU) 2022/2065

Providers of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines shall diligently identify, analyse and assess any systemic risks in the Union stemming from the design or functioning of their service and its related systems, including algorithmic systems

q: ChatGPT was designated a very large online search engine under the DSA on 31 August 2026. The consequence of that designation is that the provider must:
a: register the service in the EU database of high-risk AI systems maintained by the Commission
b: obtain a conformity assessment from a notified body before it may continue offering the service
c: assess and mitigate systemic risks, submit to independent audits and grant vetted researchers data access
d: appoint an authorised representative established in a Member State of the European Union within four months
explain: Designation follows from exceeding 45 million average monthly recipients in the Union and triggers Articles 34-37 and 40 DSA (systemic-risk assessment, mitigation, independent audit and researcher data access) under Commission supervision, applying four months after notification (Art 33(6)). Registration in the AI Act database flows from high-risk classification under that separate regime, not from a DSA designation.

sources.quote: The obligations set out in this Section shall apply, or cease to apply, to the very large online platforms and very large online search engines concerned from four months after the notification to the provider concerned
providers of very large online platforms or of very large online search engines shall, within a reasonable period, as specified in the request, provide access to data to vetted researchers

q: In 2026 the Commission referred several Member States to the Court of Justice over NIS2. That kind of referral is possible for NIS2 but not for the AI Act because:
a: NIS2 carries administrative fines, whereas the AI Act leaves the setting of penalties to national legislators
b: cybersecurity is a shared competence, whereas the internal market is an exclusive competence of the Union
c: enforcement of the AI Act is reserved to the Commission's AI Office rather than to the Court of Justice
d: NIS2 is a directive requiring national transposition, whereas the AI Act is a regulation applying directly
explain: Failure to transpose is a directive-specific infringement; a regulation needs no transposition, so no transposition deadline can be missed. Member States can still be pursued over the AI Act, but for failures such as not designating authorities.

sources.quote: By 17 October 2024, Member States shall adopt and publish the measures necessary to comply with this Directive.
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

q: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) imposes its obligations on:
a: manufacturers placing products with digital elements on the market of the European Union
b: providers of general-purpose AI models above the systemic-risk training-compute threshold
c: essential and important entities in listed critical sectors, with accountability at management level
d: online platforms with more than 45 million average monthly recipients of the service in the Union
explain: NIS2 is organisational cybersecurity: risk-management measures and incident reporting for entities across 18 sectors, with management bodies accountable. Product cybersecurity for digital products is the Cyber Resilience Act's object, not NIS2's.

sources.quote: Member States shall ensure that essential and important entities take appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures to manage the risks posed to the security of network and information systems

Member States shall ensure that the management bodies of essential and important entities approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures taken by those entities in order to comply with Article 21, oversee its implementation and can be held liable

q: The Cyber Resilience Act matters to an AI Act compliance team because:
a: it requires essential and important entities in critical sectors to adopt cybersecurity risk-management measures
b: it obliges providers to register their high-risk systems in the EU database before placing them on the market
c: it requires a fundamental rights impact assessment before a public body may deploy a product in its services
d: it sets lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements, supporting Article 15 conformity
explain: The CRA's secure-by-design, vulnerability-handling and update duties overlap with the AI Act's accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity requirement, so CRA evidence can serve Article 15. Reporting duties applied from 11 September 2026 and the full regime from 11 December 2027; risk management for entities in critical sectors is NIS2's object, not the CRA's.

sources.quote: Where high-risk AI systems fall within the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 and the conditions laid down in Article 12(1) of that Regulation are fulfilled, such systems shall be deemed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements set out in Article 15 of this Regulation.
This Regulation shall apply from 11 December 2027. However, Article 14 shall apply from 11 September 2026

q: Which is a target of the Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030?
a: 20 million ICT specialists employed in the Union, with more women entering the field
b: 75% of enterprises holding a cybersecurity certificate issued under the Cybersecurity Act
c: one AI Factory and one European Digital Innovation Hub in every Member State by 2030
d: 50% of the electricity used by data centres in the Union to come from renewable sources
explain: Decision (EU) 2022/2481 sets 20 million ICT specialists, 80% of those aged 16-74 with at least basic digital skills, 75% of enterprises using cloud, big data or AI, gigabit connectivity and full online availability of key public services. The others are plausible policy goals but are not Digital Decade targets.

sources.quote: at least 20 million ICT specialists are employed within the Union, while promoting the access of women to this field and increasing the number of ICT graduates;

q: A draft note says the EU will miss its 2030 target of 75% of enterprises using cloud, AI or big data. The most technically sound caveat to add is:
a: the target applies only to large enterprises, so weak uptake among the small and micro firms that dominate the economy does not affect it
b: the indicator is collected by the Commission directly from firms, so national figures cannot be compared
c: the target was withdrawn in the 2025 review, so no comparison against a benchmark is now possible
d: the indicator counts use of any one of three distinct technologies, so a single figure hides very different adoption rates
explain: The target is a composite: an enterprise counts if it uses cloud computing, big data or AI, and cloud uptake is far higher than AI uptake, so the headline overstates AI diffusion. Eurostat's survey covers enterprises with ten or more employees across Member States and is comparable — the weakness lies in the composite, not the sampling.

sources.quote: at least 75 % of Union enterprises have taken up one or more of the following, in line with their business operations: (i) cloud computing services; (ii) big data; (iii) artificial intelligence;

q: The AI Continent Action Plan, COM(2025) 165 of 9 April 2025, is organised around:
a: a Union-owned foundation model, procurement quotas and mandatory open weights for public bodies
b: export controls on advanced processors, investment screening and reciprocity in public procurement
c: harmonised standards, notified body capacity and a single conformity assessment procedure for high-risk systems placed on the market
d: computing infrastructure and data, adoption in strategic sectors, skills and talent, and regulatory simplification
explain: The plan is a capacity-building agenda: AI Factories and Gigafactories, access to high-quality data, sectoral adoption, skills, and simplification of compliance. Standards and notified-body capacity are real AI Act workstreams but belong to implementation of the Regulation rather than to this plan.

sources.quote: Third, we need to stimulate the further development of AI algorithms and leverage their adoption in the EU’s strategic sectors.

Fifth, the EU’s large single market is a significant asset, with one set of clear rules, including the AI Act, preventing market fragmentation and enhancing trust and security in the use of AI technologies. Nevertheless, there is a need to facilitate compliance with the AI Act, particularly for smaller innovators.

q: AI Factories under the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking are:
a: national testing and experimentation facilities certified to carry out conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems for SMEs
b: Commission-operated data centres hosting the Union's official registers and public sector language models
c: private cloud regions contracted by Member States to host sensitive public administration workloads
d: AI-optimised supercomputing sites giving startups, SMEs and researchers compute alongside data and talent services
explain: AI Factories hosted at EuroHPC sites across most Member States, together with AI Factory Antennas, provide access to EuroHPC machines with wraparound services. Testing and experimentation facilities are a separate Digital Europe instrument aimed at sectoral testing, not at compute provision.

sources.quote: “AI factory” means a centralised or distributed entity that provides an AI supercomputing service infrastructure which is composed of an AI-optimised supercomputer or an AI partition of a supercomputer, an associated data centre, dedicated access and AI-oriented supercomputing services
AI Factory Antennas will provide remote access to AI-optimised supercomputing resources of the linked AI Factory located in another Member State.

q: InvestAI, announced at the Paris AI Action Summit in February 2025, is:
a: a €20 billion Union guarantee scheme covering liability claims arising from general-purpose AI models
b: a €200 billion budget line in the multiannual financial framework reserved for grants to AI research
c: a mobilisation of around €200 billion for AI investment, including a €20 billion fund for gigafactories
d: a €2 billion instrument financing the national AI strategies coordinated through the Coordinated Plan on AI
explain: InvestAI combines public and private sources, with a dedicated €20 billion InvestAI Facility, developed with the EIB Group, targeting up to five AI gigafactories. It is not an MFF budget line: the money is leveraged from existing programmes, national contributions and private investors.

sources.quote: announced InvestAI, an initiative to mobilise EUR 200 billion for investment in AI in line with the political priorities of the Competitiveness Compass.
the launch of the InvestAI Facility, with a view to mobilise EUR 20 billion investment for AI infrastructure, notably targeting up to 5 AI Gigafactories across the Union.

q: The Apply AI Strategy, COM(2025) 723 of 8 October 2025, aims primarily to:
a: set out how AI will be used to accelerate scientific discovery across the European Research Area and its infrastructures
b: define the conformity assessment route for high-risk AI systems used by public administrations
c: create a European fund financing deployment of open-weight models inside Member State agencies
d: accelerate uptake of AI in strategic sectors and in the public sector, supported by an Apply AI Alliance
explain: Apply AI is the adoption arm of the AI Continent agenda, mobilising around €1 billion from existing programmes across sectors such as health, manufacturing, energy and defence. The science agenda is the companion AI in Science strategy, COM(2025) 724, presented the same day.

sources.quote: Introducing sectoral flagships - to boost AI use in key industrial sectors of the EU economy and in the public sector.
the Commission is mobilising around EUR 1 billion from its funding programmes

q: RAISE, the initiative announced with the EU's AI in Science strategy, is:
a: a funding instrument financing chairs for AI researchers returning to the Union from third countries, and their teams
b: a research infrastructure consortium operating the Union's exascale supercomputers for open science
c: a European register of scientific datasets made available for training general-purpose AI models
d: a pilot virtual institute pooling compute, data and expertise so that researchers can apply AI in science
explain: RAISE is deliberately virtual: it federates existing resources rather than building a new physical institute, and it is the centrepiece of COM(2025) 724. The Union's exascale machines are operated by EuroHPC hosting entities, not by RAISE.

sources.quote: the Resource for AI Science in Europe (RAISE) will pool strategic resources (i.e., funding, computing, data and talent) to push the technological frontiers of AI and harness its potential to drive scientific breakthroughs.
the Commission will further develop the concept of RAISE, including its governance structure, and launch a pilot phase

q: The Coordinated Plan on Artificial Intelligence differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: is a Council regulation setting national investment obligations on each Member State in AI research
b: is an implementing act laying down how national competent authorities coordinate market surveillance across borders
c: is an intergovernmental agreement outside the Union framework, like the Unified Patent Court system
d: is a non-binding framework aligning Member State strategies and investment, agreed in 2018 and revised in 2021
explain: The Coordinated Plan is soft coordination: joint priorities, national AI strategies and investment ambitions without legal obligation. Nothing in it binds a Member State — the binding layer arrived only with the AI Act.

sources.quote: published in December 2018 represents a joint commitment with Member States to foster the development and use of AI in Europe and to coordinate European and national efforts on AI.

That is why in 2018 the European Commission and the Member States committed to work together and adopted the coordinated plan on AI as a first step. The coordinated plan laid the foundation for policy coordination on AI and encouraged Member States to develop national strategies.
The coordinated plan provides a strategic framework for national AI strategies.

q: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: applies only to public authorities and has no bearing on how private companies develop AI systems
b: is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights through individual applications lodged directly against the parties
c: was concluded by the Union alone and does not bind any Council of Europe member state directly
d: is an international treaty open to non-European states, setting human-rights principles rather than product rules
explain: The Convention sets principles for AI activities across their lifecycle and is open to states beyond the Council of Europe (Art 31). Private-sector activity is covered: each Party chooses between applying the Convention's principles to private actors or taking other appropriate measures, and must declare its choice (Art 3(1)(b)).

sources.quote: This Convention shall be open for signature by the member States of the Council of Europe, the non-member States which have participated in its elaboration and the European Union.

how it intends to implement this obligation, either by applying the principles and obligations set forth in Chapters II to VI of this Convention to activities of private actors or by taking other appropriate measures to fulfil the obligation set out in this subparagraph.

q: Where an AI system processes personal data, the relationship between the GDPR and the AI Act is that:
a: the AI Act is lex specialis, so its data-governance rules replace the GDPR in respect of training data
b: the GDPR applies only where the system is classified as high-risk under Annex III of the AI Act
c: the AI Act covers non-personal data only, leaving personal data entirely to the data-protection regime
d: both apply cumulatively, and compliance with the AI Act does not supply a lawful basis for the processing
explain: Both apply cumulatively: Article 2(7) keeps Union data-protection law unaffected save for narrow carve-outs in Article 4a (special-category data for bias detection) and Article 59 (sandboxes), so a controller still needs a lawful basis, purpose limitation and, where required, a DPIA. The lex specialis reading is the commonest error: Article 10's data-governance duties are additional to the GDPR, not a substitute for it.

sources.quote: Union law on the protection of personal data, privacy and the confidentiality of communications applies to personal data processed in connection with the rights and obligations laid down in this Regulation. Without prejudice to Articles 4a and 59 of this Regulation, this Regulation shall not affect Regulation (EU) 2016/679

This Regulation should not be understood as providing for the legal ground for processing of personal data, including special categories of personal data, where relevant, unless it is specifically otherwise provided for in this Regulation.

q: Harmonised European standards matter to the AI Act's high-risk regime because:
a: a notified body may certify a high-risk system only where a corresponding international ISO standard already exists
b: Member States may not designate their market surveillance authorities until the standards are published
c: conformity with a standard cited in the Official Journal gives a presumption of conformity with the requirement
d: the Commission must withdraw from Annex III any use case for which no European standard has been developed
explain: Article 40 ties the presumption of conformity to standards cited in the Official Journal, which is why delay in the CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 work programme affects the whole high-risk timeline. Notified bodies can assess against the Act's requirements directly — a standard makes that cheaper and more predictable, it is not a precondition.

sources.quote: High-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models which are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 shall be presumed to be in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter

q: Compared with other jurisdictions, the AI Act's treatment of general-purpose AI models is distinctive because it:
a: requires model providers to obtain prior authorisation from a supervisory authority before any training run begins
b: prohibits release of model weights above a defined training-compute threshold to any third party
c: applies only to models developed inside the Union, leaving imported models to national rules
d: imposes binding statutory duties on model providers where most comparable regimes still rely mainly on voluntary commitments
explain: Chapter V is the first binding legal regime for model providers, covering documentation, copyright policy, training-content summaries and, above the systemic-risk threshold, evaluation and incident reporting. There is no ex-ante authorisation: obligations attach when a model is placed on the market, not before training.

sources.quote: put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790;
placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country;

q: In Commission usage, technological sovereignty in AI policy means:
a: requiring that data generated within the Union be stored and processed on Union territory by Union-based providers
b: giving Union-based providers preference in the public procurement of cloud and AI services
c: screening every foreign direct investment in companies developing general-purpose AI models
d: reducing critical dependencies in compute, cloud and models by building Union capacity while staying open
explain: The concept is capacity and resilience — the Chips Act, EuroHPC and AI Factories, InvestAI — and the Commission consistently frames it as open strategic autonomy rather than autarky. Data localisation is a much narrower measure the Union has largely avoided in its data legislation.

sources.quote: The EU is determined to avoid the fragmenation of its single market and to enhance its capabilities to reduce dependencies on critical technologies and strengthen sovereignty in cutting edge semiconductors
While access to innovative and affordable cloud services is vital for EU competitiveness, an excessive dependence on non-EU infrastructure may bring economic security risks

q: The EU's answer to AI-generated disinformation combines:
a: criminal penalties under Union law with takedown orders issued directly by the European Commission
b: mandatory provenance certificates for all online media, with strict liability for hosting providers
c: an obligation on search engines and social platforms to demote synthetic content, with fines under the Digital Markets Act
d: transparency duties on the content's provider under the AI Act with systemic-risk mitigation by platforms under the DSA
explain: Article 50 requires machine-readable marking of synthetic content by the provider and disclosure of deep fakes by the deployer, while Articles 34-35 DSA make manipulated content a systemic risk platforms must mitigate, operationalised through the Code of Conduct on Disinformation. There is no Union criminal-law layer and no Commission takedown power for this content.

sources.quote: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

ensuring that an item of information, whether it constitutes a generated or manipulated image, audio or video that appreciably resembles existing persons, objects, places or other entities or events and falsely appears to a person to be authentic or truthful is distinguishable through prominent markings

q: A ministry wants EU co-funding to set up AI testing facilities and advanced digital skills courses. The instrument designed for that is:
a: Horizon Europe, which funds collaborative research and innovation projects across the whole of the Union and beyond
b: the Recovery and Resilience Facility, which finances national reform and investment milestones
c: the Connecting Europe Facility, which finances cross-border digital and transport infrastructure
d: the Digital Europe Programme, which funds deployment capacity, testing facilities, skills and data spaces
explain: Digital Europe is the deployment programme: AI testing and experimentation facilities, European Digital Innovation Hubs, advanced digital skills and data spaces. Horizon Europe is the closest alternative but funds research and innovation rather than the roll-out of capacity.

sources.quote: In 2024, the Digital Europe Programme will also support the development of tools for testing and validation of AI models and systems, to be used in testing facilities and sandboxes.
The Commission will support training, skilling and reskilling activities in generative AI, for example by supporting dedicated masters and doctoral programmes through the Digital Europe Programme

q: A minister asks whether the EU rolled back its AI rules in 2026. The most accurate answer is that the Commission:
a: withdrew the AI Act and replaced it with a voluntary code negotiated with the main model providers
b: suspended application of the whole Act until harmonised European standards are cited in the Official Journal of the Union
c: transferred enforcement to the Member States and gave up the Commission's own supervisory powers
d: deferred the high-risk obligations and lightened documentation duties, keeping prohibitions and GPAI rules in force
explain: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 postponed Annex III duties to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028 and simplified documentation, but Article 5 and Chapter V continued to apply and the Commission retained its GPAI enforcement powers. Simplification changed timing and burden, not the substance of the prohibitions.

sources.quote: it is appropriate that the date of application of Sections 1, 2 and 3 of Chapter III is set to 2 December 2027 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, and to 2 August 2028 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I.
SMEs, including start-ups, and SMCs, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner.

q: Which body acts as market surveillance authority for AI systems used by the Union's own institutions, bodies and agencies?
a: the European AI Board, acting through its standing subgroup on market surveillance
b: the AI Office, which supervises Union bodies as well as general-purpose model providers
c: the national authority of the Member State in which the institution has its seat
d: the European Data Protection Supervisor, which may also fine Union institutions and bodies
explain: Article 74(9) designates the EDPS for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the Act's scope, with fining powers under Article 100. The AI Office is the tempting answer, but its direct supervisory mandate covers general-purpose AI models, not the institutions' own use of AI systems.

sources.quote: Where Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies fall within the scope of this Regulation, the European Data Protection Supervisor shall act as their market surveillance authority
The European Data Protection Supervisor may impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies falling within the scope of this Regulation.

q: Advanced AI developers report voluntarily against an agreed transparency framework hosted by the OECD. That framework belongs to:
a: the Council of Europe Framework Convention, whose parties report on implementation every two years
b: the Global Partnership on AI, whose member states publish national compliance reports each year
c: the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI, which collects developer disclosures from participating firms
d: the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, whose reporting framework companies began using in February 2025
explain: The Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework, launched in February 2025 and hosted by the OECD, lets organisations developing advanced AI report against the G7 International Code of Conduct. The Council of Europe Convention is a state-level treaty and imposes no reporting duty on companies.

q: Under the AI Act, a provider releasing a model under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters:
a: falls outside the Regulation's scope entirely, since nothing is placed on the Union market in return for payment
b: must notify the AI Office before release so that a systemic-risk screening can be carried out
c: gains the relief only where the model stays below the transparency threshold set out in Annex XI
d: is relieved of the technical documentation duties but keeps the copyright policy and training-content summary
explain: Article 53(2) lifts the technical documentation and downstream-information duties for genuinely open releases, but the copyright policy and public training-content summary always apply, and the relief falls away entirely for models with systemic risk. Openness is a burden reduction, not a scope exclusion.

sources.quote: The obligations set out in paragraph 1, points (a) and (b), shall not apply to providers of AI models that are released under a free and open-source licence that allows for the access, usage, modification, and distribution of the model, and whose parameters, including the weights, the information on the model architecture, and the information on model usage, are made publicly available. This exception shall not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks.

q: Which mapping of instrument to its primary object is correct throughout?
a: DSA to data intermediation; DGA to platform moderation; CRA to gatekeeper conduct; NIS2 to product safety
b: AI Act to chip supply; Chips Act to AI conformity; DGA to cloud switching; DSA to incident reporting
c: Data Act to public sector data re-use; DGA to secondary use of health data; EHDS to cloud switching; DMA to independent platform audits
d: DMA to gatekeeper contestability; NIS2 to organisational cybersecurity; CRA to product cybersecurity; Data Act to connected-product data
explain: Each pairing in the key matches the instrument's core object. The DSA governs intermediary services and platform duties while the DGA sets up data intermediation and altruism — swapping those two is the commonest mix-up.

sources.quote: laying down harmonised rules ensuring for all businesses, contestable and fair markets in the digital sector across the Union where gatekeepers are present
This Regulation lays down harmonised rules, inter alia, on: (a) the making available of product data and related service data to the user of the connected product or related service;

q: A national immigration authority plans to deploy an AI system to triage visa applications. Before putting it into use it must:
a: obtain an opinion from the European AI Board and register the system in a national database of public deployments
b: have the system certified by a notified body established in the Member State of deployment
c: publish the system's technical documentation and the datasets used to train and validate it
d: carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment and operate under its market surveillance authority
explain: Migration, asylum and border control is an Annex III area, and public bodies deploying such systems owe the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, under the national market surveillance authority (for Union bodies it would be the EDPS, Art 74(9)). A notified body is not generally required — most Annex III systems use internal control for conformity assessment.

sources.quote: AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies to assist competent public authorities for the examination of applications for asylum, visa or residence permits

Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services

q: Signing the general-purpose AI Code of Practice:
a: is mandatory for any provider whose model exceeds the systemic-risk training-compute threshold
b: replaces the Chapter V obligations for signatories until harmonised standards become available
c: has been a condition for placing a general-purpose AI model on the market of the Union since August 2025
d: is voluntary and gives signatories a recognised route to demonstrate compliance with Chapter V duties
explain: Adherence is voluntary: the Commission assessed the Code as an adequate means of demonstrating compliance, and non-signatories must show compliance by other means, which invites closer scrutiny. Meta declined to sign, and xAI signed only the Safety and Security chapter — both remain lawful positions.

sources.quote: Providers of general-purpose AI models may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with the obligations set out in paragraph 1 of this Article, until a harmonised standard is published.

Providers of general-purpose AI models who do not adhere to an approved code of practice or do not comply with a European harmonised standard shall demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance

q: The mechanism by which the Commission can add a use case to Annex III of the AI Act is:
a: an implementing act adopted after a favourable opinion of the European AI Board
b: a Commission decision published in the Official Journal after a public consultation
c: a delegated act, confined to the areas already listed and conditional on evidence of risk
d: an amendment through the ordinary legislative procedure proposed jointly with the Council
explain: Article 7 empowers delegated acts, which keeps the high-risk list adaptable without reopening the Regulation, but the Commission cannot create a new Annex III area. Implementing acts are used elsewhere in the Act — for the Scientific Panel's rules, for instance — which makes that option the plausible trap.

sources.quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI systems are intended to be used in any of the areas listed in Annex III;
The Commission shall, by means of an implementing act, make provisions on the establishment of a scientific panel of independent experts

q: The AI Gigafactory programme required a change to EuroHPC's founding regulation because:
a: the Union's own resources ceiling had to be raised to accommodate the additional capital expenditure
b: supercomputer procurement had to be moved from national authorities to the Joint Undertaking itself
c: state aid clearance could not be granted without an explicit legal base in a Council regulation
d: the Joint Undertaking's mandate had to be extended to cover AI infrastructure of this scale and purpose
explain: Council Regulation (EU) 2026/150 of 16 January 2026 amended Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 so that EuroHPC could host and procure gigafactory-scale AI infrastructure. The Joint Undertaking already procured supercomputers jointly with participating states, so no transfer of procurement competence was needed.

sources.quote: The existing mechanisms currently provided for under Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 are not sufficient to support the establishment and operation of the AI gigafactories. A targeted amendment is therefore necessary to provide the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (the ‘Joint Undertaking’) with the legal basis needed to fulfil its commitments relating to the establishment and operation of AI gigafactories in Europe.
COUNCIL REGULATION (EU) 2026/150 of 16 January 2026 amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 on establishing the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking

q: The legal basis on which general-purpose model providers currently rely for text and data mining of protected works is:
a: a dedicated exception in the AI Act covering training of general-purpose models on lawfully accessed works
b: the Database Directive's sui generis right, which permits extraction for non-commercial research purposes
c: the Data Act's provisions on access to data generated by connected products and related services
d: the exceptions in the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive, subject to a reservation of rights
explain: Articles 3 and 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 supply the text and data mining exceptions, and Article 4's machine-readable opt-out is what rightsholders use to reserve their works. The AI Act adds a duty to have a copyright policy respecting that reservation, but creates no exception of its own — assuming otherwise is the common error.

sources.quote: Directive (EU) 2019/790 introduced exceptions and limitations allowing reproductions and extractions of works or other subject matter, for the purpose of text and data mining, under certain conditions. Under these rules, rightsholders may choose to reserve their rights over their works or other subject matter to prevent text and data mining

put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790

q: Which statement about AI and EU competition policy is accurate?
a: designation under the Digital Markets Act extends automatically to every AI service a gatekeeper offers
b: acquisitions of model developers escape merger control entirely because the targets have little turnover
c: the Commission may impose interoperability duties on any model provider under competition law without first finding an infringement
d: partnerships between large platforms and model developers can be reviewed even short of a notifiable merger
explain: DG Competition is examining investments and partnerships between large digital players and generative AI developers under antitrust rules, and concentrations below the EU Merger Regulation thresholds may still be reviewed under national merger control or referred to the Commission. DMA designation is service by service: an AI assistant is covered only if it is a designated core platform service.

sources.quote: DG Competition is looking into possible vertical or other concerns relating to the investments and partnerships between large digital players and generative AI developers.

To the extent that such concentrations do not meet the turnover thresholds under the EU Merger Regulation, the Commission will work together with Member States and the parties to assess whether they will be reviewed under national merger control regimes or referred to the European Commission
Gatekeepers should comply with the obligations laid down in this Regulation in respect of each of the core platform services listed in the relevant designation decision.

q: Under the AI Act's penalty regime, the highest tier of administrative fines applies to:
a: failure by a deployer to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment, up to 6% of annual turnover
b: supply of incorrect information to notified bodies, up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover
c: failure to register a high-risk system in the EU database, up to €30 million or 6% of worldwide turnover
d: infringement of the prohibited practices in Article 5, up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover
explain: Article 99 reserves the 7% or €35 million ceiling for breaches of Article 5, with most other infringements at 3% or €15 million and supplying incorrect information at 1% or €7.5 million. The distractor figures echo the GDPR's tiers, which do not map onto the AI Act.

sources.quote: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

The supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover

q: European Digital Innovation Hubs are:
a: regional offices of the AI Office supervising high-risk AI systems used on their territory and advising national authorities
b: consortia operating the Union's AI Factories and allocating supercomputing time to researchers
c: accredited bodies carrying out conformity assessment of AI systems for SMEs at reduced fees
d: one-stop shops co-funded by the Union helping SMEs and public bodies test digital and AI technology before investing
explain: The EDIH network is the test-before-invest retail layer of EU digital policy, co-funded by the Digital Europe Programme and national sources (151 hubs selected in the 2021-22 calls; 83 renewed in October 2025). Compute access is the AI Factories' role — EDIHs advise, train and broker finance rather than operate infrastructure.

sources.quote: European Digital Innovation Hubs aim to ensure a successful digital transformation of SMEs, mid-caps and public sector organisations.
continuing to provide flanking services such as funding advice, networking and training

q: The AI Act's obligations were staged so that:
a: the high-risk duties applied first, because they had the clearest precedent in existing product legislation
b: all obligations applied together two years after entry into force, as in other internal market regulations
c: each Member State fixed its own application dates within a window laid down by the Regulation
d: prohibitions and AI literacy applied first, general-purpose model duties next, and high-risk duties last
explain: Article 113 stages application: prohibitions and AI literacy six months after entry into force, general-purpose AI and governance at twelve months, with the high-risk regime last — and pushed further out by the Digital Omnibus. Dates are fixed by the Regulation itself, leaving no national discretion.

sources.quote: Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025;
Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101;
2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and

q: Under the Safety and Security chapter of the general-purpose AI Code of Practice, a safety and security framework is expected to set out:
a: an insurance arrangement covering damage to third parties arising from downstream deployment of the model by others
b: a commitment to release model weights openly once independent evaluations have been concluded
c: a guarantee that model weights and inference operations remain within Union territory at all times
d: risk acceptance criteria tied to capability thresholds, with mitigations and a decision on whether to proceed
explain: The framework is a pre-committed decision procedure keyed to measured capability: tiers defined in terms of model capabilities, a safety margin, and an explicit determination whether to proceed with development or with making the model available. It is neither a financial nor a localisation undertaking.

sources.quote: Signatories commit to specifying systemic risk acceptance criteria and determining whether the systemic risks stemming from the model are acceptable (as specified in Measure 4.1). Signatories commit to deciding whether or not to proceed with the development, the making available on the market, and/or the use of the model based on the systemic risk acceptance determination
a high-level description of what safety and security mitigations Signatories would need to implement once each systemic risk tier is reached

q: The most defensible statement for a 2026 policy brief on AI and the EU labour market is:
a: net displacement will exceed job creation in every Member State and every sector before 2030
b: productivity gains fully offset displacement, so aggregate employment effects can safely be disregarded in planning
c: labour-market effects fall outside Union competence and cannot be addressed at Union level
d: exposure concentrates in cognitive tasks, while the size and timing of net job effects remain uncertain
explain: That is the honest reading of the evidence: the nearest-term impact falls on jobs made up mainly of cognitive tasks, while the magnitude and timing of displacement remain uncertain and net effects vary by country and sector. The other options either overclaim a uniform outcome or deny a role the Commission already takes on: monitoring AI's labour-market impact to support skills and inclusive policies.

sources.quote: General-purpose AI will likely have the most significant near-term impact on jobs that consist mainly of cognitive tasks.
General-purpose AI is likely to transform a range of jobs and displace workers, though the magnitude and timing of these effects remains uncertain.

the Commission will actively monitor the impact of AI on the labour market in order to anticipate the needs of the market, spot potential disruptions and support the development of appropriate and inclusive policies

Current general-purpose AI is likely to transform the nature of many existing jobs, create new jobs, and eliminate others. The net impact on employment and wages will vary significantly across countries, across sectors, and even across different workers within the same job.
Labour market risks arise from the potential of general-purpose AI to automate a wide range of complex cognitive tasks across sectors.

q: An EU note on AI's environmental footprint should draw its reporting data primarily from:
a: harmonised standards adopted under the AI Act covering the energy efficiency of high-risk systems and their training
b: annual sustainability reports published voluntarily by the largest cloud and AI model providers
c: product documentation required under the Cyber Resilience Act for products with digital elements
d: the data-centre reporting scheme under the Energy Efficiency Directive plus energy information in GPAI documentation
explain: Those are the two mandatory channels: data centres with at least 500 kW of installed IT power report annually to the European database under the Energy Efficiency Directive, and Annex XI of the AI Act requires the known or estimated energy consumption of a general-purpose model. Provider sustainability reports are useful but voluntary, unaudited and not comparable across firms.

sources.quote: Member States shall require owners and operators of data centres in their territory with a power demand of the installed information technology (IT) of at least 500kW, to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available
The Commission shall establish a European database on data centres that includes information communicated by the obligated data centres in accordance with paragraph 1.
known or estimated energy consumption of the model. With regard to point (e), where the energy consumption of the model is unknown

q: A tax administration ranks returns for audit selection using an AI system. The most accurate AI Act reading is:
a: prohibited, because it predicts the likelihood of an offence on the basis of profiling alone
b: high-risk, because Annex III covers any AI system that a public authority deploys in the exercise of its official duties
c: outside the Act's scope, because direct taxation remains within Member State competence alone
d: not listed in Annex III, so the deployer must still test it against Article 5, data-protection and administrative law
explain: Tax audit selection is not an Annex III use case — tax authorities are not law enforcement authorities for this purpose — so the compliance burden comes from elsewhere. The Article 5 prohibition on predicting criminal offences is the tempting reading, but it is confined to assessing the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence.

sources.quote: AI systems specifically intended to be used for administrative proceedings by tax and customs authorities as well as by financial intelligence units carrying out administrative tasks analysing information pursuant to Union anti-money laundering law should not be classified as high-risk AI systems used by law enforcement authorities

the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons in order to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person

q: Which risk is one of the specified systemic risks that a signatory of the general-purpose AI Code of Practice must always assess, with no prior screening step?
a: concentration of the market for advanced general-purpose AI models among a handful of providers
b: energy consumption of large-scale training runs and of high-volume inference serving at scale
c: infringement of copyright in the works used to train and subsequently fine-tune the model
d: loss of control over a model that can evade human oversight or resist being modified
explain: The Safety and Security chapter names four specified systemic risks — chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear; loss of control; cyber offence; harmful manipulation — which are identified automatically rather than through screening. Concentration of power and environmental effects sit in the open-ended identification process built on the five broader risk types, so they are assessed only where screening selects them.

sources.quote: the following are treated as specified systemic risks for the purpose of systemic risk identification in Measure 2.1, point (2)
Loss of control: Risks from humans losing the ability to reliably direct, modify, or shut down a model.

q: A signatory's safety and security framework must define systemic risk acceptance criteria. For a specified systemic risk, those criteria are required to be:
a: agreed in advance with the AI Office and published in full before training of the model is allowed to begin
b: derived from the compute used in training, measured against the threshold set in Article 51
c: reviewed each year by an independent auditor accredited by a national notifying authority
d: expressed as measurable tiers of model capability, including at least one tier the model has not reached
explain: The Code requires tiers defined in terms of capabilities, measurable, with a safety margin and at least one unreached tier, so the provider commits in advance to a decision point rather than judging after the fact. The criteria are the provider's own: the Commission assesses the adequacy of the Code, it does not approve individual frameworks before training.

sources.quote: are defined in terms of model capabilities, and may additionally incorporate model propensities, risk estimates, and/or other suitable metrics;
comprise at least one systemic risk tier that has not been reached by the model; or
define other appropriate systemic risk acceptance criteria, if systemic risk tiers are not suitable for the systemic risk and the systemic risk is not a specified systemic risk

q: A draft measure would treat any model trained above a fixed floating-point-operations threshold as high risk and anything below it as safe. The strongest technical objection is:
a: training compute cannot be measured after the fact, so the threshold would be impossible to enforce
b: compute figures are commercially sensitive, so providers could not disclose them without suffering competitive harm
c: the threshold would capture only models trained inside the Union, leaving imported models unregulated
d: capability per unit of compute rises with algorithmic progress, so a fixed threshold drifts from the risk it proxies
explain: A compute threshold is a decaying proxy: the same capability becomes reachable with less compute each year, and fine-tuning or scaffolding adds capability without additional training compute. The AI Act treats 10^25 operations as a rebuttable presumption and lets the Commission amend it by delegated act precisely because the proxy needs maintenance.

sources.quote: A general-purpose AI model shall be presumed to have high impact capabilities pursuant to paragraph 1, point (a), when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 1025.

to amend the thresholds listed in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, as well as to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency

q: A draft policy states that mandatory watermarking of AI-generated images will solve the deepfake problem. The most technically sound critique is:
a: watermarking works only for still images, so audio and video content could not be covered by the measure at all
b: watermarking would expose the confidentiality of the model weights used to produce the content
c: watermarking is incompatible with the transparency obligations already imposed under Article 50
d: watermarks can be stripped or degraded, and their absence cannot be read as evidence that content is authentic
explain: Detection fails in both directions: adversaries remove or forge marks, and the volume of unmarked legitimate content means absence of a mark proves nothing, so provenance has to be paired with platform-level mitigation and media literacy. Audio and video can in fact be marked, and the Article 50 duty already extends to them.

sources.quote: However, watermarking techniques face several limitations, including watermark removal by sophisticated adversaries (298*, 299) and methods for tricking watermark detectors (299).
They are an imperfect strategy for detecting AI-generated content (especially text) because they can be removed by simple modifications to data
Watermarking techniques have shown promise in helping people identify the origin and authenticity of digital media for videos (290, 291), images (292, 293, 294*), audio (295, 296), and text (297).

q: A draft rule would require every output of a deep neural network to be accompanied by a complete causal explanation of how it was produced. The soundest objection is:
a: explanations would expose the training data and so conflict with data-protection and trade-secret obligations
b: the requirement duplicates the technical documentation already owed under Annex XI of the AI Act
c: generating explanations at inference time would raise the energy cost of each query substantially
d: no such explanation exists for models of this kind, so the rule would be met only by post-hoc approximations
explain: Attribution methods approximate a model's behaviour and can disagree with one another, so a completeness requirement would be satisfied in form rather than substance. The workable drafting is the AI Act's: information meaningful for the intended purpose and for the person affected, backed by logging and human oversight.

sources.quote: AI scientists and AI developers only have a minimal ability to explain why these models made a given decision over another one, and how their capabilities arise from their known internal mathematical components.
Current ‘interpretability’ techniques for explaining the internal structures of general-purpose AI models are unreliable and require major simplifying assumptions

q: A Member State proposes that all AI inference for public bodies run on servers in its territory, so as to guarantee control over the models used. The main gap in that reasoning is:
a: inference cannot be run on national infrastructure unless the provider discloses its source code
b: Union law bars a Member State from requiring any data processing on its own territory, whatever the justification
c: national servers cannot reach the throughput large models need without dedicated accelerators
d: the location of inference says nothing about who controls the weights, the updates or the model's withdrawal
explain: Hosting determines where computation happens; it confers no rights over the model itself, so a provider can still deprecate a version, change behaviour through an update or end the licence. Control is secured contractually — version pinning, exit rights, escrow — and by access to weights, not by geography.

sources.quote: Data localisation requirements shall be prohibited, unless they are justified on grounds of public security in compliance with the principle of proportionality.

including in the field of public procurement, without prejudice to Directive 2014/24/EU, which imposes the processing of data in the territory of a specific Member State or hinders the processing of data in any other Member State

q: For technology watch on open-weight models, the distinctive feature compared with models served only through an API is that:
a: open-weight models are always smaller and so stay below the systemic-risk compute threshold
b: downstream users become providers under the AI Act as soon as they run the model on their own hardware rather than an interface
c: the provider keeps a technical means of revoking access if the model is later found to be unsafe
d: safeguards can be removed by fine-tuning after release, and a release cannot be recalled once weights circulate
explain: Irreversibility is the defining property: refusal training can be undone cheaply, and no update or shutdown reaches copies already distributed, which is why the Act's open-source relief falls away at systemic-risk scale. Running a model on your own hardware does not by itself make you a provider — that turns on substantial modification or placing it on the market under your own name.

sources.quote: these safeguards are easier to remove for open models. For example, even if an open-weight model has safeguards built in, such as content filters or limited training data sets, access to model weights and inference code allows malicious actors to circumvent those safeguards
A risk factor for open-weight models is that there is no practical way to roll back access if it is later discovered that a model has faults or capabilities that enable malicious use

q: The International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio, is best described to a non-technical audience as:
a: a negotiated intergovernmental text setting out the specific commitments that the participating states have accepted
b: an annual compliance assessment of the largest model providers against agreed safety benchmarks
c: the technical annex to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on artificial intelligence
d: a synthesis of scientific evidence on advanced AI risks that deliberately makes no policy recommendations
explain: The Report is an evidence synthesis backed by around thirty countries plus the EU, OECD and UN, and its authors stress that policy choices are for governments. Presenting it as an agreed government position is the error most likely to mislead a policy audience.

sources.quote: including an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by 30 countries, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the European Union (EU), and the United Nations (UN). The report aims to provide scientific information that will support informed policymaking. It does not recommend specific policies.
The report is the work of independent experts. Led by the Chair, the independent experts writing this report collectively had full discretion over its content.

q: In technology watch on the general-purpose AI ecosystem, which observation is the most robust basis for concern about concentration?
a: concentration in the general-purpose AI market has eased since 2024 as more providers entered
b: most of the world's most capable models are now developed inside the European Union
c: training costs have fallen far enough that a mid-sized firm could now train a frontier model of its own
d: frontier training depends on a small number of accelerator suppliers and hyperscale cloud operators
explain: Access to advanced chips and hyperscale cloud is genuinely narrow: developers depend on a few companies for GPUs, and three companies control about two-thirds of cloud computing. Concentration has not eased, most notable models in 2023 came from the US rather than the EU, and a state-of-the-art model can cost hundreds of millions of dollars to develop, well beyond a mid-sized firm.

sources.quote: Increasing dependency on prominent tech companies for access to essential hardware (GPUs), AI model interfaces (APIs), and cloud storage services
Just three companies control 67% of cloud computing services
the previous consensus that market concentration in the general-purpose AI market is high has continued to hold
in 2023, the majority of notable general-purpose AI models (56%) were developed in the US.
Market shares for general-purpose AI tend to be highly concentrated among a few players, which can create vulnerability to systemic failures.

Developing state-of-the-art, general-purpose AI models requires substantial up-front investment. For example, the overall costs for developing a state-of-the-art model can currently reach hundreds of millions of US dollars. Key cost factors are computing power
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturer and the main supplier of chips to AI hardware firms such as Nvidia

q: A provider of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk finds that the model enabled a significant cyber intrusion. Under the AI Act it must:
a: notify the national market surveillance authority of every Member State concerned within fifteen days
b: suspend availability of the model until the Commission has completed an evaluation of that model
c: inform the European Data Protection Supervisor and notify the affected data subjects directly
d: track and document the incident and report it without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national authorities
explain: Article 55(1)(c) routes serious-incident reporting for systemic-risk models to the AI Office without undue delay, with national competent authorities informed as appropriate. The fifteen-day deadline belongs to Article 73, which applies to providers of high-risk AI systems reporting to market surveillance authorities.

sources.quote: keep track of, document, and report, without undue delay, to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures to address them
not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer, becomes aware of the serious incident

q: A briefing on AI's energy footprint should note that, for a widely used model across its lifetime:
a: training dominates lifetime energy use, so limiting the size of training runs is the decisive lever
b: energy use is proportional to parameter count, so a published parameter count suffices for an estimate
c: data-centre electricity consumption is already capped for operators reporting under the Energy Efficiency Directive
d: cumulative inference can exceed the energy used for training, so deployment scale matters as much as model size
explain: High-volume serving accumulates demand that can outweigh a single training run, which is why the policy levers include data-centre efficiency and demand-side measures rather than training alone. The Energy Efficiency Directive imposes reporting on data centres above 500 kW of installed IT power, not a cap on their consumption.

sources.quote: Although reporting often focuses on the energy cost of model training, there is strong evidence that a higher energy demand arises from their everyday use.
In 2022, Google and Meta reported that the use of AI systems accounted for 60–70% of the energy associated with their AI workloads, compared to 0–40% for training

Member States shall require owners and operators of data centres in their territory with a power demand of the installed information technology (IT) of at least 500kW, to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available

q: Under the DSA, the Commission's guidelines on electoral integrity ask very large platforms to:
a: remove all synthetic media during the period between the calling of an election and the close of polling stations
b: verify the identity of every account that posts political content during an electoral campaign
c: obtain approval from national electoral authorities for recommender changes made during a campaign
d: label generative AI content in political contexts and apply provenance techniques such as watermarking and metadata
explain: The April 2024 guidelines under Article 35(3) recommend labelling and provenance signals that survive resharing, including labels on AI-generated political advertising. They stop short of removal duties or identity verification, which would raise fundamental-rights problems of their own.

sources.quote: Clearly label, or otherwise make distinguishable through prominent markings, synthetic or manipulated images, audio or videos that appreciably resemble existing persons
such as watermarks, metadata identifications, cryptographic methods for proving provenance and authenticity of content, logging methods, fingerprints or other techniques
providing advertisers with options to clearly label content created with generative AI in advertisements or promoted posts

q: The Commission's July 2025 guidelines on the protection of minors under the DSA were accompanied by:
a: a mandatory minimum age of sixteen for access to social media services across the Union
b: a prohibition on using recommender systems for accounts belonging to users under eighteen
c: a delegated act laying down binding design standards for services that are likely to be accessed by minors
d: an EU age-verification solution designed to work with the European Digital Identity Wallets
explain: The guidelines under Article 28(4) came with an EU age-verification solution designed to work with the European Digital Identity Wallets. No EU-wide minimum age was set: the guidelines recommend how to apply Article 28(1) and are not binding standards.

sources.quote: the Commission is currently testing an EU age verification solution as a standalone age verification measure

Implementation of the reference standard (43) set by the EU age verification solution can be offered through apps published by public or private entities or integrated in the upcoming EU Digital Identity Wallets.
Nevertheless, adopting and implementing the measures set out in these guidelines, either partially or in full, shall not automatically entail compliance with that provision.

q: For an AI-driven customer service chat in a bank's consumer app or in an online shop serving consumers in the Union, accessibility obligations arise principally from:
a: Directive (EU) 2016/2102, on the accessibility of public sector websites and mobile applications
b: the General Product Safety Regulation, which covers consumer products placed on the Union market
c: the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to design their interfaces free of dark patterns
d: the European Accessibility Act, applicable since June 2025 to e-commerce, banking and consumer computing
explain: The European Accessibility Act applies to services provided to consumers after 28 June 2025, including consumer banking and e-commerce, so the chat in either falls under it. The public sector website directive is the close alternative but reaches only public sector bodies' websites and apps.

consumer general purpose computer hardware systems and operating systems for those hardware systems;

This Directive lays down the rules requiring Member States to ensure that websites, independently of the device used for access thereto, and mobile applications of public sector bodies meet the accessibility requirements set out in Article 4.
