q: The latest State of the Digital Decade report projects that the Union will fall several million short of its 20 million ICT specialists target by 2030. The most defensible inference is:
a: the target should be revised downward, because the projection shows it was set unrealistically high
b: the gap will close by itself as AI tools reduce the skills needed for information technology work
c: the measurement excludes self-employed specialists, so the true figure is in reality already close to the target
d: the shortfall lies in graduate flows and reskilling capacity, so it will not close through employer demand alone
explain: The State of the Digital Decade 2026 report (17 June 2026) counts around 10.5 million ICT specialists employed in 2025 and projects about 12.2 million by 2030 — a gap of roughly 7.8 million that reflects the supply of trained people rather than weak demand. The target is fixed in Decision (EU) 2022/2481 and can be changed only by amending it, so treating a missed projection as a reason to restate the ambition confuses measurement with policy.

sources.quote: According to the baseline trajectory, around 12.2 million ICT specialists are expected to be employed by 2030, meaning that only 61% of the target will be achieved by 2030
The ICT specialist gap is even more pronounced, with 10.5 million employed in 2025, just 52% of the 2030 target of 20 million
First, the supply of new entrants remains insufficient. In 2023, the EU produced only 2.7 tertiary ICT graduates per 1 000 young people

q: A national AI strategy promises a sovereign foundation model, a public compute cluster and a dedicated ministry, but names no evaluation criteria, no procurement route and no budget beyond year two. Its weakest element is:
a: the choice to train a national model rather than fine-tune an existing open-weight model
b: the creation of a dedicated ministry rather than assigning AI policy to an existing government department
c: reliance on public compute when commercial cloud capacity could be procured far more quickly
d: the absence of any means to judge whether the investment worked or to sustain it beyond the pilot
explain: A strategy without success criteria or a funding path beyond the pilot can be neither steered nor defended, and that failure holds whatever technical choices it makes. The other three describe genuine trade-offs, each defensible depending on the country's industrial base and talent pool.

q: A company's responsible-AI policy promises human oversight of all AI decisions, internal red-teaming before each release and an ethics board meeting once a year. The most technically sound criticism is:
a: internal red-teaming is worthless unless carried out by an accredited external conformity assessment body
b: an ethics board is unnecessary where the company already complies with the Union's data-protection rules
c: the policy should commit to publishing model weights so that independent researchers can verify its claims
d: oversight of every decision is not credible at scale and invites rubber-stamping rather than genuine control
explain: A blanket oversight promise fails the way automation bias does: volume forces nominal review, so the credible commitment is oversight targeted at consequential decisions with measured override rates. Internal red-teaming is a recognised practice — its weaknesses are scope and independence, not the absence of accreditation.

sources.quote: remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias)

q: Comparing approaches to AI governance as of 2026, which statement is accurate?
a: the United Kingdom enacted a general AI statute after renaming its AI Security Institute
b: China regulates generative AI only through voluntary standards agreed with domestic providers
c: the Council of Europe Framework Convention has entered into force and now binds all of its signatories
d: the United States has no cross-cutting federal AI statute and acts mainly through executive orders
explain: US federal policy has run through executive orders and an AI action plan since January 2025, with Congress passing no cross-cutting legislation. The Council of Europe Convention is the closest trap, but it binds only Parties that have ratified it — signature alone creates no obligation to apply its terms.

sources.quote: In respect of any signatory which subsequently expresses its consent to be bound by it, this Convention shall enter into force on the first day of the month following the expiration of a period of three months after the date of the deposit of its instrument of ratification, acceptance or approval.

q: After the Digital Omnibus, the AI Act's regulatory sandbox regime requires that:
a: providers test high-risk systems in a sandbox before any conformity assessment may be carried out
b: sandboxes be operated jointly by the AI Office and the national data protection authorities
c: participation in a sandbox exempt the provider from the high-risk obligations for a period of up to three years
d: each Member State establish at least one national sandbox by 2 August 2027, with a Union-level sandbox possible
explain: The Omnibus moved the national sandbox deadline from 2 August 2026 to 2 August 2027 and added a Union-level sandbox that the AI Office may establish, with priority access for SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps. A sandbox is voluntary supervised testing: it neither replaces conformity assessment nor suspends obligations.

sources.quote: Member States shall ensure that their competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, which shall be operational by 2 August 2027.
The AI Office may establish an AI regulatory sandbox at Union level for AI systems covered by Article 75(1).
establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, which shall be operational by 2 August 2026

q: The Digital Omnibus added new entries to the AI Act's list of prohibited practices. They concern:
a: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, without judicial authorisation
b: emotion recognition in the workplace and in educational institutions outside medical or safety uses
c: untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet to build facial recognition databases
d: generating or manipulating intimate imagery of an identifiable person without consent, and abuse material involving children
explain: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 inserted prohibitions on non-consensual intimate imagery and on child sexual abuse material into Article 5(1), applicable from 2 December 2026. The other three practices have been prohibited since February 2025, which is what makes them plausible answers.

sources.quote: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts
with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026

q: A ministry uses an AI system that flags inconsistencies in benefit decisions already taken, for human review, without scoring or ranking applicants. Under the AI Act the system:
a: is automatically high risk because it is used by a public authority in the exercise of its duties
b: is prohibited, because it evaluates natural persons on the basis of their social or personal behaviour over a period
c: is outside the Regulation altogether, because the final decision is always taken by a human official
d: may fall outside the high-risk class under the derogation, but must be registered and must not involve profiling
explain: Article 6(3) lets an Annex III system escape the high-risk class where it detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, but profiling of natural persons always remains high risk and the assessment must be documented and the system registered. Deployment by a public authority is not itself the trigger — the use case has to sit in Annex III.

sources.quote: the AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review
Notwithstanding the first subparagraph, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons.

A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service. Such provider shall be subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2).

q: Presenting a model evaluation to a non-technical audience, the most honest way to convey uncertainty around a reported 92% accuracy is to:
a: round the figure down to 90% so that the audience does not overinterpret the precision of the result
b: present only the confidence interval, so that the audience sees a statistical range rather than a point
c: compare the figure with human performance on the same task, giving the audience a familiar reference
d: state the test conditions and the population it was measured on, and say where it is likely to be worse
explain: A headline metric means something only with its test set, its population and its known failure modes, which is what lets a policy audience judge whether it transfers to their setting. A human baseline is a useful device but says nothing about where the model's errors fall and misleads if it was measured under different conditions.

q: Designing AI awareness training for policy officers who will not build systems, the most useful learning objective is:
a: being able to implement a transformer architecture and train it on a small labelled dataset
b: memorising the article numbers of the AI Act's obligations for providers and for deployers
c: operating the main commercial chat assistants and comparing their outputs on policy tasks
d: recognising when a claim about an AI system needs evidence, and what evidence would settle it
explain: Article 4, as replaced by the Digital Omnibus, asks providers and deployers to take measures supporting AI literacy suited to their staff's knowledge and the context of use; for policy staff the transferable skill is critical appraisal of claims rather than engineering or recitation. Hands-on use of assistants builds familiarity but does not by itself teach anyone to judge whether a vendor's performance claim is sound.

sources.quote: Providers and deployers of AI systems shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf
This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual.

q: An SME asks where to obtain authoritative guidance on whether its product falls within the AI Act. The service created for that purpose is:
a: the European Digital Innovation Hub network, which advises SMEs on adopting digital technologies
b: the Scientific Panel of Independent Experts, which advises on general-purpose AI model risks
c: the European AI Board, which issues opinions on consistent application of the Regulation
d: the AI Act Service Desk and single information platform, the Commission's single entry point for AI Act questions
explain: The Service Desk is the single entry point for AI Act questions, with an explorer, a compliance checker and a helpdesk aimed at SMEs and start-ups. EDIHs advise on adoption and the AI Board coordinates national authorities — neither answers an individual firm's classification question.

sources.quote: a hub to access all relevant information about the AI Act, navigate its content, understand how it applies and get tailormade answers to any question related to its implementation. It includes a single information platform with interactive tools, in particular a compliance checker
the Commission is launching the AI Act Service Desk, which will be a central information hub on the AI Act, allowing stakeholders to ask for help and receive tailor-made answers

q: The Data Union Strategy presented in November 2025 responds to which diagnosis?
a: European data centres lack the capacity to store the datasets needed for frontier model training
b: data-protection rules prevent any use of European personal data for machine learning purposes
c: Member States apply divergent data localisation requirements to public sector information holdings
d: the Union's data rules are fragmented and high-quality data is hard to access for training AI models
explain: The strategy targets simplification and consolidation of the data acquis plus better availability of high-quality data for AI, on the view that complexity and fragmentation are the binding constraint. Storage capacity is a separate problem addressed by the compute and cloud strand of the AI Continent agenda.

sources.quote: to respond to the scarcity of robust and high-quality data for the training and validation of AI models
Particular attention will be given to streamlining existing data legislation to reduce complexity and administrative burden

q: The Cloud and AI Development Act, as proposed by the Commission in 2026, would:
a: require providers of general-purpose AI models to host their model weights on infrastructure located in the Union
b: oblige Member States to procure compute capacity exclusively through the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking
c: set binding energy efficiency limits for data centres above a defined installed power threshold
d: expand Union data-centre capacity and add a cloud sovereignty framework conditioning public procurement
explain: The proposal aims to multiply EU data-centre capacity and to create assurance levels for cloud sovereignty that gate public-sector procurement, with Union added value as a non-price award criterion. It is a proposal in the ordinary legislative procedure, not law, and imposes no localisation duty on model providers.

sources.quote: It aims to triple EU capacity in the next five-to-seven years and reach the needed capacity by 2035, while ensuring balanced geographic deployment across Member States.

Where a risk assessment determines that the activities of such contracting authorities have public order relevance, they must only procure and use services that have been recognised as offering Union assurance levels 2, 3, or 4.
